name: Victor Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. So you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a transmission crew, so the big steel towers, not the poles on your street. We meet at the depot by the river at six, do the tailboard briefing, which is the safety talk at the back of the truck, and then drive out to wherever the job is. This month it's replacing insulators on a line that runs along the motorway, so we're harnessed up eighty metres off the ground half the day. I love the view and I love the crew, but my shoulders tell me every morning that I'm fifty-eight.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out the most, apart from the shoulders?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Waiting, honestly. Waiting for the outage to be switched, waiting for permits, waiting for the helicopter. I fill a lot of that time on my phone, I'll admit. I use an AI app to sort the drone photos of the towers, and I get it to tidy up the notes I write for the union branch, because my spelling's terrible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I say now: it's a handy tool and that's all. At the branch meeting I'd tell people to stop worrying and start asking the company where the time savings are going. If the app saves us an hour on paperwork, I want that hour showing up somewhere, not just in a manager's bonus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means not much for me. I've got about five years left, a decent pension coming and money put by, so if nothing radical happens I just ride it out. Part of me would be a bit disappointed, to be fair, because I like the gadgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keeps going, basically. I'd keep using the photo app and keep showing the younger ones how to use it, and I'd push the branch to get a line in the next agreement about sharing any productivity gains. Ines and I would stick to the plan, which is the caravan and the coast when I finish at sixty-three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, maybe, like a film that promised a big ending and then just stopped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use AI to sort drone photos. Would that change in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd still use it. It flags rust and cracked insulators faster than I can squint at a screen. Last spring it spotted a split on a tower near the quarry that three of us had missed, so I'm not giving that up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the crew would be happiest with this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Dennis, without a doubt. He's sixty-one and still writes his job notes in a paper book with a pencil stub. He'd be down the pub saying he told us so, and he'd be right, for once.

S0.say: It's a handy tool and that's all it is, so people can stop worrying. The real question is where the time it saves us ends up, and I'd want that in the next agreement.
S0.think: Honestly, it means very little for me, with about five years left, a pension coming and money put by. I'd be a bit disappointed, because I like the new tools.
S0.do: Keeps using the drone photo app and teaching younger crew members to use it. Pushes the union branch to ask for a share of any time savings in the next agreement, and sticks to the plan of retiring at sixty-three.
S0.feel: Calm, with a slight sense of anticlimax.
S0.quote: Last spring it spotted a split on a tower near the quarry that three of us had missed, so I'm not giving that up.
S0.fieldNote: Victor is the rare older lineworker who is a fan of the tools, and his first instinct is a union one: who keeps the savings. He sounds almost let down by a world where nothing changes. His security is solid and he knows it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Like before, I'll read the card first. This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming whether we like it or not, so let's be at the table instead of on the menu. At work I'd tell the lads to learn the tools now, because the ones who can run them will be the ones they keep. Online I'd probably share something about the unions in other industries that got deals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I think I'm fine. Climbing a tower in the wind isn't something a computer does next year. The bit I'd worry about is the office side of our company, the planners and dispatchers, and my son Owen, who tests software for a bank in the city.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer for whatever pilot the company runs, probably the drone inspections or the new fault-finding software, because I'd rather shape it than have it handed to me. I'd put a motion to the branch asking for a joint committee on new technology within the first six months. And I'd sit down with Owen and talk through what he could move into, maybe chip in for a course if he needs it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, a bit of an itch about Owen. I don't lie awake over it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which tasks on your crew do you think would go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Inspections, for sure. Right now we walk the line or fly it once a year and someone squints at photos. That'll be drones and software doing it every month. Then maybe the planning, working out which crew goes where. The actual hanging of wire and changing of insulators stays with us for a good while yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd want retraining money. Who should pay for it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The company, and the government should make sure they do. They're the ones saving the money. I'd want a training fund written into the agreement, paid per head, so it's there for the dispatcher who's forty-five and suddenly finds half her job's on a screen she doesn't control.

S1.say: It's coming whether we like it or not, so we should be at the table instead of on the menu. Learn the tools now, because the people who can run them are the ones who'll be kept.
S1.think: I think my own job is safe, because a computer isn't climbing a tower in the wind any time soon. My worry is the office side of the company, and my son Owen, who tests software for a bank.
S1.do: Volunteers for the company's pilot of drones or fault-finding software and puts a motion to the union branch for a joint technology committee within six months. Talks with his son about other paths and offers to help pay for a course.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, with a small worry about his son.
S1.quote: It's coming whether we like it or not, so let's be at the table instead of on the menu.
S1.fieldNote: He sees himself as safe and turns straight to protecting others, both at work and at home. He trusts collective bargaining more than the market to share the gains. There's no gap between what he'd say and think here, which fits someone this comfortable with change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd be the one calling for an emergency meeting. I'd say workers and governments need to move now, not after the robots are already on the towers. I'd be on every forum asking what the plan is, because there won't be one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be all right, money-wise. Ines and I own the house, the savings would carry us, and I'm close enough to pension age that I could just step off. But I'd feel like I was leaving the young lads on the crew to drown, and Owen's job would be gone before mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start running the numbers on retiring at sixty instead of sixty-three, because if a robot can climb that tower by 2028 they'll offer packages and I'd want the best one. I'd go hard on the union side, pushing for redundancy terms and for the company to keep a human on every live job for safety. And I'd move some of our savings to help Owen while he works out what's next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not for me so much. It's that feeling when you're on the ground watching someone else on the tower and the wind picks up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is very short. What would you do in the first month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get everyone in the branch room, frankly. I'd want our demands written down before the company writes theirs. Then I'd book an appointment with the pension people to see exactly what I'd lose by going three years early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be about sixty when it arrives. Does that make it easier or harder?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Easier for me and that's the uncomfortable part. Two years means I just squeak through. If you're thirty and you've got a mortgage, two years is nothing. You can't retrain as anything because there's nothing it can't do. I'd feel almost guilty being able to walk away.

S2.say: Workers and governments need to move now, not after the robots are already on the towers. I'd call an emergency meeting and keep asking what the plan is, because there won't be one.
S2.think: I'd be all right for money, with the house paid off and savings behind us. But I'd feel like I was walking away while the young crew members and my son were left to sink.
S2.do: Runs the numbers on retiring at sixty instead of sixty-three and books a meeting with the pension office in the first month. Pushes the union for redundancy terms and a rule keeping a human on every live job, and sets aside savings to support his son.
S2.feel: Anxious on behalf of others, with some guilt that he can walk away.
S2.quote: Two years means I just squeak through. If you're thirty and you've got a mortgage, two years is nothing.
S2.fieldNote: The short warning splits his fate from the people he cares about, and he feels that sharply. His own plan is retirement, but his energy goes into the union. The guilt at being one of the lucky ones was the most honest moment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same end point now, but more time. This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been given a warning, so use it. I'd be telling people to get the government to set up a proper fund for workers before 2031. Five years is a full bargaining cycle, so there's no excuse for being caught out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2031 I'm sixty-three, which was my plan anyway. So for me it lines up almost too neatly. What I really think is that this is the version where people like me get lucky and everyone younger has a short, rough run-up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in the job to sixty-three as planned. I'd ask to be on the team that tests the climbing robots or the drones that string wire, because I'd rather see how good they really are. And I'd spend my union time on a transition deal, with retraining, early pensions and a say in how fast the machines come in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than worried. It's a known date, and I like a known date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the extra three years buy you, compared with 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time for the branch to win something real. With two years you're just negotiating your own funeral. With five you can get training paid for, agree a pace, maybe get the company to keep apprentices on. There'll still be jobs the robots can't do for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you train with the robots if the company asked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, in a heartbeat. I'm the one who already argues with the photo app when it's wrong. If something's going to be on a tower near live wire, I'd want someone who's been up there thirty years checking what it does, not a graduate in an office.

S3.say: We've been given a warning, so we should use it. Five years is a full bargaining cycle, and the government should set up a proper fund for workers before 2031.
S3.think: By 2031 I'm sixty-three, which was my plan anyway, so it lines up almost too neatly. This is the version where people like me get lucky and everyone younger has a short, rough run-up.
S3.do: Stays in the job until sixty-three as planned and asks to join the team testing climbing robots or wire-stringing drones. Spends his union time on a transition deal covering retraining, early pensions and the pace of change.
S3.feel: Uneasy rather than worried, reassured by having a clear date.
S3.quote: With two years you're just negotiating your own funeral. With five you can get training paid for, agree a pace, maybe get the company to keep apprentices on.
S3.fieldNote: The extra years turn him from protester to negotiator, which suits him better. He keeps coming back to the young crew and apprentices. He actively wants to work beside the machines rather than avoid them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty if we stop arguing about whether it's real and start planning. I'd push for it in the union paper and probably at the ballot box too, voting for whoever's serious about a fund for retraining and shorter hours. People should be able to share the gains, not just lose their jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It doesn't touch me directly. I'd be long retired, probably on the coast in the caravan, fixing the neighbours' fences. I really think it could be good, if it's done fairly. That's a big if.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the next five years as normal and keep mentoring the young ones on the tools. I'd help set up a training scheme through the union so apprentices learn to work with the robots, not just against them. Outside work I'd vote and campaign for a fund that shares the gains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit hopeful, to be honest. It's the only one where there's time to get it right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be doing in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably on a beach complaining about the weather. Maybe teaching a night class on line safety, if anyone still needs one. I'd like to think some of the robots up those towers were checked by people I trained.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you say anything different to your grandchildren, or your kids, in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Owen and Maya that the tools aren't the enemy, it's who owns them. I've said that for years. With ten years, they'd have time to get on the right side of that.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty if we stop arguing about whether it's real and start planning. I'd push for a retraining fund and shorter hours, in the union paper and at the ballot box.
S4.think: It doesn't touch me directly, since I'd be retired on the coast by then. I think it could actually be good if it's done fairly, but that's a big if.
S4.do: Works the next five years as normal while mentoring young crew members on the new tools. Helps set up a union training scheme for apprentices to work alongside robots, and votes and campaigns for a fund that shares the gains.
S4.feel: Calm and somewhat hopeful, because there's time to get it right.
S4.quote: I'd tell Owen and Maya that the tools aren't the enemy, it's who owns them.
S4.fieldNote: This is the scenario he finds hopeful, and he frames it in terms of ownership and fairness. He moves smoothly from his own retirement to institutions like training schemes and policy. A consistent, optimistic progressive who likes the machines but not the bosses.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028. Not for me, I'd be fine, but for the lads on my crew in their thirties and for Owen. What would help is a deal agreed in advance: early pensions for people near the end, paid retraining for the rest, and the company not allowed to put a robot on a live line without a person signing it off.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who I trust. I trust the crew and I trust the branch, and I'd trust a decent government. I don't trust anyone who tells me the machines will just sort it out by themselves. I've seen what happens when we leave the line to the contractors.

headlineQuote: I love the view and I love the crew, but my shoulders tell me every morning that I'm fifty-eight.
portrait: Victor Walsh is a 58-year-old transmission lineworker who climbs steel towers out of a riverside depot and is also his union branch's keenest gadget user. He already uses AI to sort drone photos and tidy his union notes, and he'd happily test climbing robots himself. With a paid-off house, savings and retirement planned at sixty-three, he is personally secure in every scenario, so his worry runs to the younger crew and his son Owen, who tests software for a bank. He grows anxious only with AGI by 2028, where he would retire early and feel guilty for squeaking through, and he becomes hopeful with ten years' warning. Throughout, he insists the tools aren't the enemy; who owns them is.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, not for himself but for the younger lineworkers on his crew and for his son.
whatWouldHelp: A deal agreed in advance, with early pensions for people near the end, paid retraining for everyone else, and a person required to sign off any robot working on a live line.
